findings.title: Local cache is populated before the DB write, so a rejected device is let through on its next request
findings.body: `tagDeviceUI` calls `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})` and only afterwards calls `anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice`. With the new device limit, `CreateOrUpdateDevice` can fail with `ErrDeviceLimitReached`, which `Authenticate` turns into an authentication failure. However the cache key for that device has already been stored (29 minute TTL), so the very next request from the same device hits `if _, ok := a.localCache.Get(key); ok { return nil }`, `TagDevice` returns nil, and `Authenticate` succeeds. In practice the limit only blocks the first request; a page refresh bypasses it for ~29 minutes, after which the cycle repeats. The cache entry must only be set after a successful store write (or be removed on `ErrDeviceLimitReached`). This pattern was harmless before because tagging was best-effort, but it now defeats the feature.

findings.title: Count-then-insert is not atomic; concurrent new devices can exceed the configured limit
findings.body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` reads `CountDevices(...)` and then, if `count < deviceLimit`, performs the upsert in a separate session. There is no transaction, lock, or conditional insert tying the two together, so N concurrent first-time devices (e.g. a burst of new visitors, or several Grafana instances each with an empty local cache) all observe `count < limit` and all insert, leaving the table above the limit. If the limit is intended as a hard cap (licensing/abuse control) this needs either a serialized check-and-insert (e.g. `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < ?` or the existing `serverlock`), or the docs should state that the limit is best-effort.

findings.title: Device limit is only enforced for requests that volunteer the X-Grafana-Device-Id header
findings.body: `TagDevice` returns nil immediately when the `X-Grafana-Device-Id` header is absent, and `Authenticate` then grants the anonymous identity. Because the header is entirely client-controlled, any client (scripts, curl, a browser with the header stripped) can use anonymous access without ever being counted or limited, so the new `device_limit` setting cannot be relied upon to cap anonymous usage. If the limit is meant to be an enforceable cap, requests without a device id should either be rejected when a limit is configured or be subject to a separate check; otherwise the limitation should be made explicit in the setting's documentation.

findings.title: ProvideAnonDBStore signature change is not reflected in the wire provider set
findings.body: Before this change `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` received an `anonstore.AnonStore` via dependency injection, which means the server wire set had to contain a provider for it (`anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` plus a `wire.Bind(new(anonstore.AnonStore), new(*anonstore.AnonDBStore))`). This PR changes `ProvideAnonDBStore` to take an extra `deviceLimit int64` and constructs the store manually inside `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService`, but no change to `pkg/server/wire.go` is included. If the old provider/binding remains, `wire` generation fails (no provider for `int64`, and an unused `AnonStore` binding), breaking the build; if it is silently removed elsewhere, that change should be part of this PR so reviewers can verify it.

findings.title: updateDevice mutates captured args inside a closure that WithDbSession may retry
findings.body: `updateDevice` does `args = append([]interface{}{query}, args...)` inside the callback passed to `WithDbSession`. `WithDbSession` re-invokes the callback on SQLite `locked`/`busy` errors (`retryOnLocks`), so on a retry the query string is prepended a second time and `dbSession.Exec(query, query, clientIP, ...)` is executed with one bind parameter too many, which fails and makes every retry attempt a guaranteed error. Build the full argument slice outside the closure (or inside it from a fresh slice) so retries are idempotent. The same pattern exists in `CreateOrUpdateDevice`, but this PR introduces it anew in `updateDevice`.

findings.title: Device-limit tests cover only the rejection path, not the update-at-limit path or the service/cache layer
findings.body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that a second new device gets `ErrDeviceLimitReached` at the store level. There is no test that an already-known device is still accepted (and updated) once the limit is reached, which is the main behaviour `updateDevice` exists for. There is also no test in `impl_test.go` that exercises `TagDevice` with a non-zero `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit`, and no test of `Anonymous.Authenticate` returning an error for a rejected device; a service-level test issuing two requests from an over-limit device would have exposed the local-cache bypass described in another finding.

findings.title: New auth.anonymous.device_limit setting is not added to defaults.ini/sample.ini or the configuration docs
findings.body: A new `[auth.anonymous] device_limit` key is read here, but the PR does not add it to `conf/defaults.ini`, `conf/sample.ini`, or `docs/sources/setup-grafana/configure-grafana/_index.md`. Grafana's convention is that every setting appears in defaults.ini (so `grafana cli admin` / settings pages show it) and is documented, including the semantics of `0` meaning unlimited and what users experience when the limit is hit. Without this, operators have no discoverable way to learn the option exists or how it behaves.

findings.title: ErrDeviceLimitReached is a plain error, so rejected users get a generic unauthenticated response with no explanation
findings.body: `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is defined with `fmt.Errorf` and is returned straight out of `Anonymous.Authenticate`. The authn/contexthandler layers only surface `errutil` errors with status codes and public messages; a plain error becomes a generic 401/redirect-to-login, and the authn service also logs a warning for every request from the rejected device. End users hitting the limit see a login page with no indication why anonymous access stopped working, and operators get noisy warn logs. Define it as an `errutil` error (e.g. `errutil.TooManyRequests`/`Unauthorized` with a public message) so the frontend can show a meaningful message, and consider lowering the log level for this expected condition.
